If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content: "129 :     public MultiKey(final K[] keys) {\n130 :         this(keys, true);\n131 :     }"

Title: Diagnosis
Details: 
- The failing test serializes and deserializes a subclass of MultiKey (DerivedMultiKey) and asserts that the hashCode remains the same after the round trip.
- In MultiKey, the hashCode field is declared transient (private transient int hashCode;), so it is not serialized. It is computed in constructors via calculateHashCode(...) and returned in hashCode().
- Because constructors are not called during deserialization, MultiKey relies on a readResolve() method to recompute the transient hashCode after deserialization. The current implementation defines:
  - private Object readResolve() { calculateHashCode(keys); return this; }
- This setup works for MultiKey itself, but fails when deserializing a subclass (DerivedMultiKey). The reason is that the readResolve method in MultiKey is private, and thus is not inherited by subclasses. During deserialization of the subclass, the private readResolve in the superclass is not invoked, leaving the transient hashCode at its default value (0).
- As a result:
  - Original object (mk): hashCode correctly computed in constructor.
  - Deserialized object (mk2): hashCode remains 0 because readResolve was not invoked for the subclass.
  - The assertion mk.hashCode() == mk2.hashCode() fails.

This matches the current bug report: after the fix for COLLECTIONS-266, MultiKey uses a transient hashCode and readResolve, but with subclassing this fails because readResolve is private. To support subclassing, readResolve should be declared protected (or MultiKey should be final).

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
